title: Grace Aguilar
hook: a nineteenth-century English Jewish writer and teacher

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was learning grows: two women over one page of Talmud, and torat imecha, your mother's Torah. Did you learn something from a woman who knows more than you? Today ends the week with a writer. Day one thousand forty-three.

A young woman in England, at a desk, with a Bible open and a pen in her hand. She is Jewish, from a family whose ancestors, the family remembered, had once hidden their Judaism in Portugal to survive. Around her, English Jewish girls are growing up reading English books. And some of the books about the Bible they can read in their own language were written by people hoping to persuade them to leave Judaism. She has a simple thought: our women should hear the Bible's women from one of their own. Her name is Grace Aguilar, and she picks up the pen.
screen: `A DESK IN ENGLAND.` → `A FAMILY THAT ONCE HID.` → `SHE PICKS UP THE PEN.`

segments.voice: Grace Aguilar lived in the nineteenth century, and she wrote in English, for English-speaking Jews. She wrote novels, poems and books of religious teaching. In a book called The Spirit of Judaism she wrote about faith as something felt and lived in the heart and the home, not only kept by rule. In another, The Women of Israel, she went through the Bible woman by woman: Sarah, Rebekah, Miriam, Deborah, Ruth, Hannah, and on, telling their stories for Jewish women readers. Part of her point was an answer. Some writers of her day claimed that Judaism held women low. She went back to the text and said, in effect: look at these women. Look at how the Torah speaks of them. A verse from the last chapter of Proverbs fits the whole project: "She openeth her mouth with wisdom; And the law of kindness is on her tongue." She also wrote a novel, The Vale of Cedars, about Jews in Spain who had to hide their faith, the history her own family carried. And she taught: with her mother she kept a small school for boys at home. Her health was poor, and she died young, while traveling in Germany. Her books kept being read after her. Now look back at the week. The women who were always there. A seamstress who started a school. A rabbi in Berlin. A girl at a lectern. The debates that continue. Learning that grows. And today, a writer. Each one, in a different room, made her own place inside the tradition, and wanted it heard. A woman's voice.

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: read one woman writer. Sit comfortably, and let your breath slow. Think of a book, a poem, an essay or even a letter written by a woman that has stayed with you. Bring back one line or one image from it, as best you can. Let it sit in you. If nothing comes, that's an answer too: it may be time to find one. Grace Aguilar's books are old enough that you can find them free. Before the bell, choose what you'll read today, even if it's just one page. The bell holds the time.
Grace Aguilar. The nineteenth-century English Jewish writer and teacher who retold the women of the Bible for Jewish women, in their own language. Today's word.
Your line: a woman's voice. Today, read one page by a woman writer, and let her have the last word in your head tonight. Day one thousand forty-three.

howItsDone: Grace Aguilar's books are read today in Jewish women's history and literature courses, and her retellings of biblical women are studied as an early example of Jewish women interpreting scripture for one another.
